If this is too long for you just skip to the "TL;DR" below. So naturally there's been some concern lately about whether voat is going to end up a more "right" or "left" site politically speaking. As many have pointed out, this shouldn't really concern people as long as no one who is backing up their arguments is censored. But what's bothered me is that many intelligent people are still identifying strictly as "right" or "left". So I figured I'd write a little bit about the distinction and propose an alternative for anyone who's interested.

What does it even mean to be right or left. (The one dimensional spectrum)

Look at an example chart like this. There's some things we might disagree with like "equity" being right and "equality" being left but for the most part it's a decent example. But is being right wing solely mean that you want to keep things as they are? If so that would make 'conservative' and 'right wing' synonyms which they most certainly are not. Wikipedia in my opinion offers a much more concise and consistent definition. Left wing is in opposition to social hierarchy where as right wing believes that such hierarchy is either beneficial or inevitable. This puts both fascism and anarcho-capitalism on the right, with communism and social democracy on the left.

The two-dimensional spectrum.

Surely everyone here has seen this chart here from the political quiz, right? It is essentially an attempt to address the massive amount of pidgin holing that occurs when you split all of politics into one big binary. It has two axis, libertarian/authoritarian and left/right. The left/right still more or less represents what the Wikipedia articles said they did, but now we've basically got a second axis that tells us how much a particular ideology/person wants to force said hierarchy or lack thereof on people. Traditional fascism goes in the authoritarian center-right, anarcho-capitalism in the libertarian right, communism in the libertarian left, and socialism in the authoritarian left.

Why I dislike this.

While I've certainly taken that quiz before and think it's much better than a one axis system I still think it's not really the best way of representing politics. Remember how above the right believed that "hierarchy is beneficial or inevitable"? Well the strict right-left spectrum doesn't represent the distinction between beneficial hierarchy and inevitable hierarchy at all. The two-axis does however, putting "inevitable hierarchy" on the libertarian right and "beneficial hierarchy" on the authoritarian right. The problem I have here is that there is no such analogue for the left. If you believe there should not be a hierarchy how can you argue whether or not the hierarchy is beneficial or simply inevitable. You can't, because in the ideal system of the left there is an attempt to remove the hierarchy.

The alternative

So basically this alternative of mine removes the defunct distinction in the left-wing and distills the remaining three extremes based on their supposed values. Now this isn't a totally original concept, if you look up "political triangle" I'm sure you'll eventually find something like this. Anyway, I made this excellent and very professional graph after hours in a very exclusive photo editing software, here. Additionally I made one with American Republicans, American Democrats and the average European style social democrat overlayed onto it, here. Obviously these are crude averages/guesses but it should get across the idea that the main distinction between republicans and democrats is one of "how hard should we work to make everyone equal" whereas social democracy veers a bit in the other direction to sacrifice ideals like patriotism or militarism in exchange for equality and maybe a little liberty.

A note on the origin of the right-left dichotomy

As many will tell you the distinction and the terms started in the French revolution but that's not what I want to make note of here. I just wanted to reinforce how the first past the post voting system we have does indeed limit us to two major parties and it is based on this that we have such a binary limiting distinction in politics. I'd just like to think that in places like Voat where we don't have to confine ourselves to mainstream American politics we can consider how absurd the binary they have forced us into is.

TL;DR

The right represents support for hierarchies whereas the left is for the dissolution of hierarchies, but does not distinguish between the belief that hierarchies are simply inevitable and the belief that they are actually beneficial. I have crudely drawn up how I personally see politics here. Thanks for reading if you did.

Speaking of nationalism

As for nationalism, that's an interesting question and the first thing I should say is that the definition of nationalism a self-described nationalist is going to use is going to be different from the layman's definition. To most people who have heard the term they often think of it as basically a pejorative for "patriotic". That is it is the "bad" form of patriotism. Obviously I reject this definition. The unintuitive part is that the "nation" in nationalism is not the nation-state but rather refers to a collective people and culture. This is how things like "black nationalism" or various separatist movements can exist and still be nationalist while rebelling against their government.

The nationalist wants his people to be united with certain values and have these common values preserved yet there are a few basic variants. First, there is "ethnic" nationalism which is the idea that people of a certain race/ethnicity should stick together for their own self-preservation. This is what you get in a lot of Europe where there is any nationalism to speak of. Obviously Nazi Germany would have been this. There's also "civic" or "cultural" nationalism. This eschews the racial aspect and essentially believes anyone who contributes and follows the common values can be accepted as a member. I would argue Mussolini's fascism was closer to this but also this is what you're going to get in America considering its immigrant history.

To specifically address your question, yeah sure libertarians could be nationalist. They would form communities of voluntary association with like members and admittance to the group would be based on acceptance of the communities customs, values, and goals. I'm not really sure that the 'red' side of the chart can really do nationalism though. I mean yeah there's "left-wing nationalism" but that's really just a more progressive 'cultural' nationalism than full on hierarchy bashing. There's things like "queer nationalism" but despite the strange focal point is essentially similar to ethnic nationalism. Neither of these really go too close into the red side as far as I'm concerned.

I'd argue that nationalism in any form is going to bring you closer to the blue side but "free association nationalism" is certainly an interesting concept. I do believe "national anarchism" describes this but I don't know much about it.

Maybe you're right; it's difficult to see how the classical left-wing ideologies could also be nationalist. After all, Marxism explicitly rejects it by calling for a global workers unity regardless of nation, and many similar ideologies implicitly accept the same ultimate goal.

Perhaps the question of nationalism is in fact a subset of the more general question of equality (or lack thereof) as you originally posed: those on the red side would say that all nations are or should be equal and united, while those on the blue side would say that the existence of separate nations (whether based on ethnicity, culture, ideology, or some combination) is inevitable, desirable, or both. I suppose you'd get some disagreement from those in the green camp, but they'd probably also be inclined to accept that proposition.

You group communism and socialism together, this is a common misconception popular among social conservatives. Communism is a one-party system with complete state control. Socialism (more appropriately called democratic socialism), is where a strong democracy exists, and the government fundamentally exists for the betterment of the people (protection against monopolies, money influencing politics, etc). Socialists, or democratic socialists, are not against hierarchies, they are a fundamental part of a capitalist society. Some people just have the desire to become great businessmen, while others don't. And that's fine, that's the way it has always been and always will be.

The problem socialists have with hierarchies is that they can get out of control in an unrestrained laissez faire, capitalist society. This ends up hurting the average man, which severely limits their ability to succeed in life.

Communism according to Marxist theory is vastly different from what it became under the totalitarian regimes of Stalin and Mao after WWII. Ideally, a communist society calls for the most localized forms of governments, with workers controlling the means of production and with little or no state control. Total state control under a one party system is clearly in opposition to that, but it is unfortunately what modern civilization is most familiar with when concerning communism.

The right vs left debate always leaves me frustrated. I have never fit into any one point on the left/right spectrum. As soon as people identify with one side or the other they disengage themselves from objectivity and seem to lose all empathy. I see this even in myself. I'm very invested in gender egalitarianism, for both sexes...I used to be a lot more objective about misogyny than I am now, sadly...but in today's world of SJWs and witchhunts for "RedPillers" has made it difficult to take anyone decrying misogyny seriously, especially when they use Feminist-Party-Approved-Terms like 'problematic', 'toxic', or 'privilege'. A scanning electron microscope (SEM) needs samples to be coated in a thin layer of metal (gold) to be able to scan them, it's called sputtering. This is normally (always?) done in a vapor deposition chamber, which this is.
